content:
Hello,
I'm nos, location Finland. I'm quite new to Lean and I'm learning it by having AI translate my mathematical intuitions into something that, somehow, compiles without being too sorry and then I know that something at least wasn't formally an error. I don't have an academic background other than a student number at a math faculty from 20 years ago, but this stuff is still very close to my heart. At that entry exam I got everything wrong except the last question, which was dressed up to look like it was much harder than it actually was and perhaps that tells you everything you need to know about me. :smile_cat:

Today I'm here because the AI told me to show up. Not because my math is interesting but because I found a bug in the parser. My math is is interesting though and I hope to find someone who at least has time to run it through their own AI for a smoke test!
What is the bug in the parser? Can you post a #mwe please?

Martin Dvořák said:

What is the bug in the parser? Can you post a #mwe please?

Sure:

/-
 +/-1
-/

Messages (1)
MathlibDemo.lean:13:2

unterminated comment

More information and workaround:

020_lean_doc_comment_lexer_bug.md
For an MWE, nothing. - I simplified the example.
This looks like a nested comment that is not closed.
In the "intended" comment, there is a nested /- that opens a nested comment and so there are 2 layers of comments, but only one is closed.

This:

/-
±1
-/

Would be the preferred way to write this comment but most keyboards lack a chord for the unicode symbol.

As per the markdown documentation this is the workaround:

-- +/-1
The shortcut \pm should allow you to type ± in an editor with an appropriate Lean plugin.
Do you know of a more general solution? This has been a bother for a long while with many symbols.

What do you mean by general solution? Are you not using the Lean VS Code plugin (or an alternative for a different editor)? With the Lean VS Code plugin, you can type most symbols you want using short abbreviations like \pm, \to, \a, \mapsto, \<>

Something like this:
https://userbase.kde.org/Tutorials/ComposeKeyp
https://cyberborean.wordpress.com/2008/01/06/compose-key-magic/

The plugin's UX is more extensible, but not portable. There is another issue with multiple similar-looking glyphs having a different unicode addresses, so it's not a guarantee that this gets me the ± from the right charset. It's a bit of a mess IMO, which is why I'm asking if anyone has found a sustainable solution.
The thread #Editors & UIs > Unicode math input via OS instead of editor may be relevant
